text: A prisoner defends his manuscript by staging a play in the cell, with his accusers drafted as the cast. The dungeon is Spain in the sixteenth century, the Inquisition has already made its arrest, and the inmates have run a mock trial of their own with the aim of burning whatever Cervantes carried in. Arthur Hiller lets the two worlds share one floor: knight, squire, windmill and inn assembled from costume, makeup and whatever the prison provides. Songs carry a good part of it, and the film's Academy Award was for their score. What holds the two hours and twelve minutes together is the audience inside the frame, men who owe the performer nothing, who can stop the show whenever they like, and who have to be won line by line.

The film's own credits call it The Personal History, Adventures, Experience, & Observation of David Copperfield the Younger. Two hours and ten minutes are allotted to all of that, so compression is the craft problem, and George Cukor's 1935 answer shows in the cutting; the Academy's editing award went here. A boy is handed between households and trades; the money is always someone else's; kindness turns up from people with no standing to offer it. The novel's anger about class survives in small practical forms: what a child is worth as labor, what a family will tolerate to stay respectable. Nothing is allowed to linger, and the effect is closer to memory than to chronicle. Faces do the connective work a narrator would otherwise do, and the picture trusts them to carry a decade across one cut.

Roderick Usher has decided that his bloodline is tainted, and acts on the decision by trying to stop his sister's wedding. Sixty-three minutes, silent, France in 1928: dread has to be carried by image alone, by the condition of a house, the speed of a figure crossing a room, the time a door takes to open. Jean Epstein brings Madeline's fiancé Allan up to the estate the way any guest arrives, and from there the place does most of the explaining. What Roderick is willing to do to keep the marriage from happening turns cruel quickly, and La Chute de la maison Usher is more interested in the reasoning that permits it than in shocks. A curse, here, is a household condition. It is kept up daily, like damp, and it has been kept up for generations.

The chairman dies mid-meeting and, by pure accident, the one Black man on the board is left running the advertising agency. Robert Downey Sr. gave it eighty-five minutes in 1969, the right length for a comedy with no interest in letting anyone down gently. The industry under examination sells language for a living, which lets the film work at the scale of the pitch, the account, the slogan that survives a meeting, a trade where sincerity is a line item. The accident is doing double duty: it is a plot device and a remark on how such jobs are usually filled. Swope's promotion is the premise rather than the joke; the joke is what everybody does next, upstairs and down, on the phone and in the corridor. It sits on the National Film Registry now, an unlikely address for something built to behave like a stunt.

A manufacturing company without a head is still a company: orders arrive, plants run, someone has to sign. The stroke arrives without warning, and the vice-presidents must settle the succession while the ordinary week keeps landing on their desks. Robert Wise takes a hundred and four minutes and stays mostly indoors, where the argument is conducted in production runs, share price and private debt. An Academy Award went to the black-and-white art direction, and that is not decoration: the film reads men by the rooms they have been given and the ones they want. Nobody is a villain in any usable sense. Each candidate has a coherent theory of what the firm exists to do, and the theories are incompatible, which is why the vote matters more than the eulogy.

Leo and Ulrich have been friends since boyhood, which the film treats as the durable fact and the romance as the accident. Leo sees Felicitas on a railway platform, coming home from military training, and that is enough; a scandal follows and he is sent away for three years. Clarence Brown made it in 1927 without dialogue, so the arithmetic of who is looking at whom has to be exact: proximity, held glances, a hand that arrives somewhere before its owner has decided anything. The friendship gets the same close attention as the courtship, which is what makes the homecoming difficult rather than merely awkward. A hundred and twelve minutes, and the National Film Registry keeps it. Nothing here is settled by declaration; it is all conduct, and the conduct is legible from the back row.

The Adams household is split down the middle: the father and son are content behind a drugstore counter, the mother and daughter are not. Alice works the small-town ladder with the only tools available to someone without money, invitations half-extended and fully accepted, snubs absorbed, an air of having noticed nothing. George Stevens gives this ninety-nine minutes and very little slack. When Arthur appears the campaign escalates: the mother pushes the father into a business venture he never wanted, and a dinner is arranged to present the family as something it is not. The lead performance took the Academy Award for Best Actress, and it needs the range, since Alice is performing almost continuously herself. Every step upward is paid for in cash or in dignity, generally both.

Maria and Jose reach Los Angeles in the 1930s, marry, and face deportation before the decade is done. A hundred and twenty-eight minutes have to cover three generations after that, so each stretch takes only what it needs: the house in East L.A., the children, Chucho, Paco, Memo, Irene, Toni and Jimmy, caught in the fifties between youth culture and the police, then a narrowing in the sixties onto Jimmy, his marriage to Isabel, a refugee from El Salvador, and their son. Gregory Nava organizes by generation rather than by plot, so the same street and the same rooms come back with different people standing in them. The Academy Award the film carries is for makeup, a practical note: the same faces are asked to hold sixty years of weather.

The wagons are pointed at Oregon, and the trail itself is the film's real subject. Breck Coleman, hired as scout, carries three errands along one road: get the train through, make himself agreeable to Ruth Cameron, and find the men who killed his friend. A hundred and twenty-two minutes for a journey commits Raoul Walsh to the journey, so arrivals are rare and nearly everything happens in transit, at the pace a wagon sets. Courtship conducted that way has long silences built into it, and so does revenge. A wagon train is slow, and the film accepts the slowness as its subject rather than its problem. The killing Coleman means to settle waits in the past, and the road decides when it comes up. Made in 1930 and kept by the National Film Registry, it treats plain distance as an event.

Every frame in it was shot by someone else, and most of that footage was paid for by the United States government. Jayne Loader's 1982 assembly draws on instructional and reassurance films of the forties and fifties, material produced to persuade the public that an atomic weapon was a manageable feature of ordinary civic life. The sequencing carries the argument. Nothing has to be added on top of a state explaining, in its own level voice, why there is not much to fear. Eighty-six minutes, and the people on screen are not actors playing officials; they are officials, and the cheerfulness was policy. The National Film Registry now holds it, which closes a circle: government footage, re-cut into evidence, filed back into the national record.

He was slapped in public once, by the baron who had already taken his research and his wife; now a Paris sideshow pays him to be slapped nightly, in front of a crowd that finds it funny. Victor Sjöström keeps the whole thing to seventy-two minutes, and the act supplies a built-in rhythm: the laughter arrives on schedule, and so does the humiliation it is buying. A showgirl in the same company holds his attention, and her father means to marry her to the baron, the same baron, which turns a nightly routine into rehearsal for something the clown is in no position to prevent. Silent, 1924, and bleak under the greasepaint. The ring turns out to be a good place to watch a man work out how much of himself he can sell as comedy.

The reporter covering the mayor's last campaign is his nephew, and his usual beat is sports. Frank Skeffington runs a New England city on favors, memory and personal contact, and he intends one more term. By 1958 television is where people get their information, and the men with money have decided they would prefer a candidate they can handle; neither development has any use for the way Skeffington works a room. John Ford gives the campaign a hundred and seventeen minutes, time enough for its retail business and for a young man to learn what his uncle actually does all day. The conspiring happens elsewhere, in rooms with better furniture. The film will not pretend the old method was tidy, only that it required standing in the same place as the voters.

She sings to the puppets because there is nobody else to sing to, and forgets for a while that there are hands inside them. Lili Daurier is stranded in a strange town when a circus troupe takes her in; the magician who rescues her first has entanglements already and sees a child where she would rather be seen otherwise. The crowd that collects around a private conversation turns it into an act, and the act turns into wages, a living made out of the one thing she was doing for herself. Charles Walters holds the film to eighty-one minutes, which suits a situation that would not survive much explaining. The Academy Award for Best Actress went to the lead, and it is earned in the hardest available place: making a two-way conversation out of wood and cloth.

Sixteen minutes, two sailors, and an argument over which of them is the most remarkable, extraordinary fella. Sindbad has an island and a menagerie to support his claim; he wrecks Popeye's ship, carries off Olive Oyl, and then, rather than simply fighting, proposes a series of tests. That structure gives the short its shape, boast to challenge to escalation to boast, and the running time lets the menagerie become scenery instead of a single gag. Dave Fleischer's 1936 cartoon took the Academy Award for animated short film, and the reason is visible in the island itself, built to be looked at while the plot goes about its business. Popeye's resilience is both the running joke and the mechanism; the comedy lies in how long the film makes him wait to use it.
